interactions.label: Rajan presents with fever, pharyngitis, a palmar rash, and oral ulcers two weeks

params.question: Rajan presents with fever, pharyngitis, a palmar rash, and oral ulcers two weeks after a high-risk exposure. His standard HIV antibody test is negative. Why is this result expected, and what test should be ordered next?

answers.text: The antibody test is falsely negative due to immunosuppression; repeat the same test in one week

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In acute HIV the immune system has not yet mounted an antibody response — this is the window period, not an immunosuppression artefact. Repeating the same test within days will still miss the diagnosis.

answers.text: Antibodies have not yet formed during this window period; a fourth-generation combination assay detecting p24 antigen should be requested

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. During the window period (2–4 weeks post-exposure), antibodies are absent but p24 antigen circulates at high levels. The fourth-generation assay detects both, narrowing the diagnostic window to 18–45 days.

answers.text: HIV has been excluded; a Western blot should be ordered to confirm the negative result

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A Western blot also relies on antibody detection and would be negative during the window period. A negative antibody test does not exclude acute HIV when the clinical picture is suggestive.

answers.text: The antibody test is reliable at this stage; the presentation is most likely Epstein–Barr virus mononucleosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: EBV mononucleosis does not typically produce a palmar rash or oral ulcers — two features that distinguish acute retroviral syndrome. The negative monospot test already excluded EBV in this case.

overallFeedback.feedback: During acute HIV seroconversion (2–4 weeks post-exposure), antibodies have not yet formed — this is the window period. Standard antibody tests will be negative. The fourth-generation antigen–antibody combination assay detects p24 antigen and is the appropriate next investigation.

The window period is when a patient is most contagious yet hardest to diagnose. The fourth-generation combination assay bridges this gap by detecting p24 antigen directly, even before antibodies appear.

params.question: An HIV-positive patient with a CD4 count of 80 cells/µL presents with three weeks of worsening headache but surprisingly little neck stiffness on examination. Which opportunistic infection best explains this presentation?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PCP is a pulmonary infection presenting with exertional breathlessness, dry cough, and bilateral ground-glass infiltrates on imaging — not a CNS presentation.
Primary CNS lymphoma typically appears at CD4 <50 as a single ring-enhancing lesion with focal neurological deficits, not as subacute headache with minimal signs.

Correct. Cryptococcal meningitis occurs at CD4 <100 and classically presents with weeks of subacute headache. Neck stiffness is minimal because meningeal inflammation requires immune cells that are now depleted.

Cerebral toxoplasmosis presents with acute focal neurological deficits and seizures, with multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia — a different clinical picture from subacute headache alone.

overallFeedback.feedback: At CD4 <100, cryptococcal meningitis presents with weeks of subacute headache. The hallmark diagnostic trap is minimal neck stiffness — the depleted immune system cannot mount the meningeal inflammatory response that would normally produce classical signs.

The absence of classical meningism in advanced HIV is a diagnostic trap. The depleted immune system cannot mount the inflammatory response that produces neck stiffness, so its absence does not rule out meningitis.

params.question: In an infant under 18 months born to an HIV-positive mother, a reactive rapid antibody test confirms HIV infection in the infant.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Maternal antibodies cross the placenta and persist in an infant's blood for up to 18 months. A reactive rapid antibody test in this age group may simply be detecting the mother's antibodies, not the infant's own immune response. The correct diagnostic test is HIV DNA polymerase chain reaction.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. Maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and persist in the infant's blood for up to 18 months, rendering all antibody-based tests unreliable in this age group. HIV DNA polymerase chain reaction, which detects proviral DNA in the infant's own cells, is the definitive test for early infant diagnosis.

interactions.label: A 35-year-old patient is newly diagnosed with both HIV and pulmonary tuberculosi

params.question: A 35-year-old patient is newly diagnosed with both HIV and pulmonary tuberculosis. His CD4 count is 40 cells/µL and anti-tubercular treatment has just been started. When should antiretroviral therapy be initiated?

answers.text: Within two weeks of starting anti-tubercular treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When the CD4 count is below 50, the mortality risk of delaying ART outweighs the risk of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome. National guidelines recommend starting ART within two weeks of initiating ATT in this setting.

answers.text: On the same day as anti-tubercular treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Starting ART simultaneously with ATT carries a high risk of overlapping toxicities, drug interactions, and severe IRIS. A brief deferral of up to two weeks allows the anti-tubercular regimen to stabilise first.

An eight-week deferral applies when the CD4 count is above 50 (where IRIS risk outweighs the mortality risk of brief delay) or in tuberculous meningitis. At CD4 <50, this delay is too long and risks death from immunosuppression.

answers.text: After completing the full six-month anti-tubercular course

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Waiting six months to start ART in a profoundly immunosuppressed patient would expose them to life-threatening opportunistic infections. The Treat All policy mandates prompt ART initiation.

overallFeedback.feedback: In HIV–TB co-infection with a CD4 count below 50 cells/µL, the risk of death from delayed ART outweighs the risk of IRIS. Antiretroviral therapy should begin within two weeks of starting anti-tubercular treatment. At higher CD4 counts, a longer deferral of up to eight weeks is acceptable.

ART timing in TB co-infection is stratified by CD4 count: below 50 cells/µL, start within 2 weeks; above 50, defer up to 8 weeks. Tuberculous meningitis always requires 8 weeks of deferral regardless of CD4.

params.question: Ramesh, an HIV-positive patient on ART, asks whether he can ever safely have unprotected intercourse with his wife. His viral load has been undetectable for eight months. What is the evidence-based counselling response?

answers.text: No — barrier protection is always mandatory regardless of viral load

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While barrier methods protect against other sexually transmitted infections, the U=U evidence shows that a sustained undetectable viral load eliminates sexual HIV transmission. Insisting on mandatory barriers ignores current evidence and undermines adherence motivation.

answers.text: Only if his wife also takes daily pre-exposure prophylaxis with tenofovir and emtricitabine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PrEP is recommended for HIV-negative individuals at ongoing high risk, but U=U means that an undetectable viral load alone prevents sexual transmission. Requiring PrEP on top is not evidence-based in this context.

answers.text: He should wait until his CD4 count rises above 500 cells/µL before considering this

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The CD4 count reflects immune recovery, but it is the viral load — not CD4 — that determines transmissibility. A sustained undetectable viral load is the criterion for U=U, regardless of the CD4 count.

answers.text: Yes — a sustained undetectable viral load means he cannot sexually transmit HIV to his partner

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Undetectable = Untransmittable (U=U) principle is supported by robust evidence. This message transforms motivation: taking a daily tablet directly protects the people the patient loves.

overallFeedback.feedback: The Undetectable = Untransmittable (U=U) principle states that a patient who maintains a sustained undetectable viral load cannot sexually transmit HIV. This evidence-based message is central to prevention counselling and transforms adherence motivation.
U=U is a cornerstone of HIV prevention counselling. Connecting daily adherence to protecting loved ones is the most powerful motivational tool available to the clinician.
